newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong Newspaper Headlines-Feb 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong Newspaper Headlines-Feb 17.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- MING PAO -- Members of the World Trade Organisation agreed on a deal to liberalise the world's telecommunications market. In Hong Kong, it was expected that prices for mobile phones and international phone calls would come down.

-- WEN WEI PO -- Chief executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa said he would finish drawing up a name list for his new government and submit it to Beijing. Once it was approved, the list would be made public.
-- China would strengthened economic legislation to guarantee healthy and stable development of the market economy.

-- SING TAO DAILY -- The defection of a top North Korean official has not been reported in mainland media because they had been instructed by Beijing to remain silent on the news. Sources said Beijing was unlikely to send the defector back to North Korea for fear of damaging its international reputation.

-- ECONOMIC TIMES -- A company under China's Ministry of Power Industry was planning to seek a listing on Hong Kong's stock exchange. But it was studying whether the listing would affect provincial light and power companies which had already been listed in China.

-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- Britain's foreign secretary Malcolm Rifkind accepted there was little his government could do now to reverse China's decision to establish a provisional legislature in Hong Kong and repeal human rights laws. -- A report warned that Asian economies were doing too little to open up their financial sectors and the region could pay heavily for shunning reforms.
-- China saw parallel and competitive development by domestic and foreign-funded car-makers as the key to a strong mainland car industry.
-- HONGKONG STANDARD -- The Mass Transit Railway Corp announced plans for a web of new lines in Hong Kong and Kowloon and another cross-harbour tunnel.
-- Analysts said that Hong Kong stocks could slide further before buying began after a shakeout last week pummelled the Hang Seng Index to a two-month low.
